entry.title: Nepal zoo bird flu outbreak raises alarm for national parks
entry.content:
KATHMANDU — In the village of Pithauli, on the edge of Nepal’s Chitwan National Park, a safe feeding site for critically endangered vultureshas long been hailed as a success storyby conservationists.

For visitors, the feeding site, also known as a “vulture restaurant”, provides a rare photo op for tourists: As white-rumped vultures (Gyps bengalensis) and slender-billed vultures (Gyps tenuirostris) feed on carcasses laid out by locals, greater one-horned rhinos, jackals, wild boars and crows watch and, sometimes, participate.

For ornithologist Rajendra Suwal, however, this ensemble is an eyesore, he told Mongabay, “If an infected bird comes to the site, the disease could spread to other birds or even animals.”.

Suwal’s concern stems from a recent outbreak of bird flu or avian influenza in the country’s capital.An outbreak that started in mid-June at Kathmandu’s Central Zoois believed to have cost the lives of at least 65 animals and birds across more than 20 species. The dead included barn owls, Himalayan griffons, greylag geese, jungle cats, leopard cats, a sarus crane and two common leopards.

An investigation by the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC), which manages the zoo, says the origin of the outbreak could likely be traced to two sources: Among birds, it likely started through feral crows roosting in open-topped aviary enclosures, while for carnivores, it spread through chicken meat fed to them by the zoo.

Notably, the zoo’s six tigers (Panthera tigris) were unaffected. A member of NTNC’s investigation committee told Mongabay that this is not necessarily because one species is more resistant. “Tigers at the zoo are fed roughly 5-7 kilograms of buffalo meat each per day, not chicken, so they were never on the same exposure pathway as the infected carnivores,” said the committee member, who asked not to be named as they weren’t authorized to talk to the media.

In national parks, however, carnivores often share common diets. There are also no enclosures to inspect, no feeding records to audit and no vet team to notice the first death, ornithologist Suwal said. Central Zoo lost many animals before it could contain the outbreak, but a park may not know it has an outbreak at all, he added.

Read more at Mongabay Nepal

entry.title: Nepal’s newest national parks drive tiger recovery, but new concerns arise
entry.content:
KATHMANDU — Nepal is now home to an estimated 429 wild tigers, up from 355 four years ago and nearly four-fold from 16 years ago, the country’s conservation officials reported on the occasion of World Tiger Day.

As the country celebrates this historic achievement, a closer look at the latest numbers reveals an uneven recovery. Nepal’s youngest national parks are driving nearly all the growth, while Bardiya, the country’s second-oldest park, has fewer tigers. This could lead to more conflict between not just people and tigers, but people and leopards as well in and around the new national parks, according to recent studies.

Three factors appear to be behind this split: water availability, animal movement both within and outside the country, and spread of invasive species.

“The results from the survey reflect the positive outcomes of ongoing efforts in the field of tiger conservation in Nepal, such as habitat conservation and management, poaching control, conservation of prey species, and biological corridor conservation,” said Bed Kumar Dhakal, spokesperson for the Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation.

Chitwan, the country’s oldest national park, still leads by far in raw numbers. But the newer parks (Banke, Parsa and Shuklaphanta) are where growth is concentrated, while the country’s two oldest parks, Chitwan and Bardiya, are showing the slowest growth or an outright decline.

The numbers are rooted in a global pledge made in November 2010. With wild tiger numbers at an all-time low at roughly 3,200, leaders from the world’s 13 tiger range countries gathered in St. Petersburg, Russia, for the first international tiger summit, where they signed the St. Petersburg Declaration and committed to double the global wild tiger population by 2022. Nepal, then home to an estimated 121 tigers, accepted the pledge and met it by reporting 355 tigers in 2022.

A cursory reading of the latest survey data suggests that while older parks are reaching stagnation, newer ones are emerging as areas of potential growth, said researcher Saneer Lamichhane, a PhD candidate at the wildlife ecology and conservation department, University of Florida, U.S.

Read more at Mongabay Nepal

entry.title: A shy bird found only in Nepal is waiting for the world to notice
entry.content:
Nepal’s shrubby hillsides are home to a medium-sized bird with brownish upperparts, distinctive black streaks from the shafts of its feathers and, sometimes, a chalky white facial patch.

It’s the spiny babbler (Turdoides nipalensis), a mysterious bird, recorded only in Nepal. In June, the bird made headlines with asighting for the first timein the forests of Madhesh province, in Nepal’s southern lowlands. With this recording, the bird has now been spotted in all of Nepal’s seven provinces.

In Kathmandu, sightings of the bird have been recorded from the fringes of Shivapuri Nagarjun National Park to the foothills of Phulchowki, as well as at various locations in and around Pokhara, usually at an elevation ranging from915 to 2,135 meters(3,000 to 7,000 feet) above sea level depending on the season. But in June, ornithologists Hathan Chaudhary and Suraj Baral identified the bird in Madhesh for the first time, at an elevation of around 443 m (1,450 ft). This sighting means the spiny babbler has now been documented across all of Nepal’s seven provinces.

Despite its limited known habitat, the spiny babbler remains poorly understood and researchers and ornithologists are calling for greater global attention to study and protect it.

“We still don’t know a lot about the bird and have no scientific data to back its population, movements, exact breeding season/months and the effects of increasing human settlements,” said Kamal Raj Gosai, who heads the department of environmental science at Kathmandu’s Tri-Chandra Multiple Campus. Gosai is researching the distribution of spiny babbler and the impacts of land use and climate change on the species. “There’s more focus on vulnerable and endangered species and megafauna, and little concern and limited research on this endemic species, both nationally and globally,” he added.

British naturalist Brian Houghton Hodgson first scientifically described the spiny babbler,kade bhyakurin Nepali, in 1836 while living in Kathmandu. His encounter with the one-of-a-kind bird remained a one-off for more than a century, until the 1940s, when Desiree Proud, the wife of a British diplomat, spotted them in her Kathmandu garden and American ornithologist Sidney Dillon Ripley sighted the species in far-western Nepal, confirming its existence.

Read more at Mongabay Nepal

entry.title: Living with leopards in the Himalayas
entry.summary: Living with leopards in the Himalayas
entry.content:
This story was originally published by Knowable Magazine.

In the afternoon of February 22, 67-year-old Bulal Maharjan, a farmer living on the outskirts of Kathmandu, Nepal, was sitting on his porch chopping cauliflower leaves to feed his chickens. Hearing a loud thud as a parked motorcycle toppled, he turned and watched in horror as a leopard leapt away from the fallen vehicle and lunged at him, piercing its sharp canines into his forehead, its claws lacerating his hands.

Within seconds, neighbors swarmed in, and the leopard ran into a nearby house. They eventually trapped the animal inside. After nearly two hours of panic that saw two more people injured trying to control the distressed big cat, forest division officials managed to sedate it and bring the situation under control.

Maharjan still can’t shake off memories of the attack. “For three days straight, I couldn’t even sleep. Every time I began to doze, the scene of this attack would jolt me up!” he says. “I think we should just get rid of this animal. Period.”

Bulal Maharjan, 67, narrowly escaped a harrowing encounter with a common leopard outside his home on the outskirts of Kathmandu.

Sentiments like Maharjan’s are common across Nepal, where leopards have been responsible for significant loss of human life and livestock. Research shows that in the Himalayan nation from 2000 to 2020, conflicts between humans and four large mammals — elephants, rhinos, tigers and common leopards — claimed 887 human lives and led to the killing of 1,139 animals. Of these, common leopards —Panthera pardus— were the leading cause of human deaths at an average of19 deaths per year, and the species most frequently killed.

To try to bring the conflict under control, Nepal and other countries with human-large predator conflicts are exploring a range of solutions.

Nepal has three ecological zones: lowland dominated by Bengaltigers, mountainous regions where snow leopards roam free, and the vast mid-hill ruled by common leopards as the top predator. While protected areas in the lowlands and mountains receive dedicated conservation funding for their charismatic predators, the mid-hills are largely managed as community forests.

Read more at Kathmandu Post

Monkey vs machine: Nepal tests AI to fight crop-raiding macaques
entry.content:
KATHMANDU — At dawn in Birta Deurali village of Kavrepalanchok in central Nepal, maize fields aren’t quiet. Farmers stand guard, scanning the trees for movement, but they aren’t the only ones there.

“If you leave even for a short time, the monkeys do considerable damage,” said 46-year-old Sagar Tamang, a resident of Birta Deurali. Villagers take turns guarding fields every two hours, beating drums and sending dogs to chase them away.

Nepal’s macaque crop raids are making national headlines, and the country’s researchers are testing artificial intelligence-based detection and deterrence systems, though even the scientists building them admit the technology isn’t yet a reliable fix.

“We even hide food indoors, but they still find their way in,” Tamang said. “Only fire scares them now,” he added, referring to the burning sticks villagers’ wave to keep the monkeys at bay.

For farmers such as Sunmaya Lama, 32, of the same village, the losses are adding up. “We lost maize worth 30,000 rupees (about $230) this year,” she said. “Over the past three years, it has reached around 90,000 rupees (about $670).”

When she approached the local government, she said she was told there was no provision for compensation. “So we just bear the loss ourselves,” she said.

The scale of the problem extends beyond the village. A2022 nationwide analysispublished in theJournal of Environmental Managementused species distribution models to map human-rhesus macaque conflict across Nepal. It found that nearly 44% of the country’s land area contains suitable macaque habitat, with less than 8% of that within protected national parks. About 15% of all land where human settlement is permitted is characterized by moderate or high rates of conflict.

More recent research illustrated another trend. A2026 studyin theAmerican Journal of Primatology, based on a year-long field study of a macaque troop in central Nepal, found that nearly half of their diet now comes from cultivated crops. From the moment a seed sprouts until it reaches the storage, researchers said, monkeys can damage crops at every stage.

Read more at Mongabay Nepal

entry.title: Nepal’s birdwatchers can fill gaps in conservation data
entry.content:
Nepal’s expanding birdwatching community offers a vital lifeline for both biodiversity monitoring and ecotourism,reportscontributor Bibek Bhandari for Mongabay.

According to arecent study, a growing interest in birdwatching, particularly among younger generations, is helping bridge gaps in ecological data while promoting Nepal as a birdwatching destination.

Nepal is home to more than 900 bird species, including the endemic spiny babbler (Turdoides nipalensis). Of these, 172 species are nationally threatened owing to urbanization, infrastructure development and climate change.

The study surveyed 135 birdwatchers and found that only 37% shared their observations on citizen science platforms, such as eBird, or with bird conservation organizations, while 46% kept their records private. This lack of participation limits the overall impact of citizen science on regional conservation efforts, the study said.

Hem Bahadur Katuwal, study co-author and an assistant professor at China’s Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, said  birdwatchers should record their observations of the species they spot, the number of individuals seen and where they saw the birds. These data are helpful in conservation, he said.

“This helps in fulfilling the data gaps related to bird population and habitat,” Katuwal said. He added that the records also help researchers like him in assessing species’ risk levels for Nepal’s national Red Data List.

Beyond science, birdwatching presents an untapped economic opportunity for the country. While some birdwatchers spend up to 40,000 rupees ($260) per trip, according to the study, the travel sector remains dominated by trekking and religious tourism, said Ishana Thapa, CEO of Bird Conservation Nepal.

Thapa argued that proactive government promotion of Nepal as a birdwatching destination is essential. “This is a low investment that can bring great benefits to our tourism sector,” Thapa said.

A former hunter turned birdwatching guide and tourism leader, Shankar Tiwari now holds a top ranking for unique bird sightings in Nepal on eBird. Tiwari, who said he recently documented three species for the first time in Nepal, said he views his work for bird conservation as a form of restitution for his past.

Read more at Mongabay Nepal

entry.title: Scientific & traditional knowledge are key for effective & community-centered conservation (commentary)
entry.content:
A group of women often climbs steep cliffs to set up camera traps for snow leopards around Kibber in Spiti Valley, India. The senior women know the landscape intimately, like what areas the animals use and where cameras are likely to capture movement. They have walked these mountains all their lives and know how to navigate the most rugged and inaccessible terrain safely, even in snow and ice. This is a kind of access that visiting researchers simply cannot replicate.

Back at the village, they gather around two computer screens. The younger women, who are typically more adept at handling technology, organize and sort the photographic data. Together, they identify individual snow leopards from their coat patterns, building scientific monitoring skills over time. Their work contributes directly to regional and global assessment and monitoring of snow leopard populations.

Who are these scientists conducting camera-trap monitoring of snow leopards? They are not trained researchers. They are women from the Indigenous community of Kibber in Spiti Valley. This work is done alongside their other chores: Livestock rearing, farming, household responsibilities, and community work. They do this, because they are interested in knowing how many snow leopards they are helping protect on their community lands; they take pride in learning research techniques; and they see themselves as part of the global effort to study and protect them.

Lobzang Yangchen, the coordinator of the Kibber team of 11 women, says, “I started as a volunteer because I was curious about snow leopards. Now it has become my livelihood. There isn’t much else to do during winters, so this is when we do the camera trapping work.”

These women work alongside trained researchers and conservation practitioners in a genuine partnership. Their community has spent decades building conservation initiatives. When research showed that wild herbivore populations were kept low by limited availability of forage, they set aside more than 35 square kilometers (13.5 square miles) of pasture — over 20% of their total land — as a livestock-free reserve. As a result,populations of blue sheep, the snow leopard’s primary wild prey, are now five times greater than before.

Read more at Mongabay Nepal

Nepal’s Rhino translocation success in numbers masks habitat struggles
entry.summary: Nepal’s Rhino translocation success in numbers masks habitat struggles
entry.content:
While Nepal’s efforts to revive its rhinoceros population is hailed as a conservation success, habitat degradation is forcing translocated rhinos to wander far beyond their designated release zones, according to anew study,reportscontributor Bibek Bhandari for Mongabay.

The population of the vulnerable greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis)in Nepal grew by 16.6% between 2015 and 2021, reaching a total of 752 individuals. To expand the range of rhinos, authorities also established new rhino populations in Bardiya and Shuklaphanta national parks. Bardiya, which had no surviving rhinos until the early 1980s, now has about 38 rhinos, according to thelast census in 2021.

To see how the reintroduced rhinos use habitat in Bardiya, researchers attached GPS collars on five rhinos moved from Chitwan National Park to Bardiya in 2016-17. Their tracking showed that the rhinos maintain unusually large home ranges in the park’s Babai Valley. The study authors said that the behavior is likely due to fragmented riverine forests, limited grassland and seasonal water scarcity.

Study co-author Babu Ram Lamichhane, currently associated with the nonprofitWild Care Nepal, said that massive floods in 2015 and 2017 inundated the Babai Valley, reducing the grassland patches and wallowing sites rhinos require for thermoregulation and skin maintenance.

Lamichhane said during the dry season, a lack of water in the Babai River forces rhinos to travel long distances, sometimes even crossing into India.

“The rhino habitat is not at an optimal level in Babai Valley,” Lamichhane said.

As rhinos seek resources outside the core park area, they are increasingly being sighted in community forests and farmlands, where locals said the animals are involved in sporadic incidents of human-wildlife conflict and destruction of crops.

entry.title: Himalayan pangolin emerges as distinct species, 189 years after first described
entry.summary: Himalayan pangolin emerges as distinct species, 189 years after first described
entry.content:
KATHMANDU — The animal Brian Houghton Hodgson saw looked almost like a pangolin, but it didn’t tick all the boxes. It had amor-like scales from head to tail, just as the French zoologist Georges Cuvier had earlier described. But it also had ears and far more scales across its trunk than any recorded species.The year was 1836. For the 35-year-old British diplomat and pioneering naturalist, who was confined to Nepal’s Kathmandu Valley, this demanded an investigation: Was it a new species, or just an outlier?Convinced he had come across an undescribed species, he gave the animal a name built entirely on those ears,Manis auritus: The Latinauritustranslates to “with large ears.” But he hedged it with a backup name,Plurisquamis, “the many-scaled,” in case the ears turned out later to be an unremarkable feature.Nearly two centuries later, his question finally has a plausible answer. A team of scientists spanning Asia, the Americas and Europe has spent five years building the case that the pangolin Hodgson described in 1836 is in fact a separate species, distinct from the Chinese pangolin (Manis pentadactyla) it had long been lumped together with and the seven other recorded species.

Theirrecently published findingsalso establish its name, now called the Himalayan pangolin, and carry immediate consequences for conservation. Across their Africana and Asian ranges, they’re all endangered, so heavily targeted for illegal trade that they’re considered the most smuggled mammals on Earth. They are killed for their meat as well as scales under the guise of traditional medicine.Reaching consensus on taxonomy took a string of smuggling busts and decades of independent research by different teams working without knowledge of each other. In the end, it was Hodgson’s own words, and an almost two-century-old museum specimen, that sealed the case for the Himalayan pangolin.

entry.title: Nepal’s birdwatchers help monitor wildlife and promote tourism
entry.summary: Nepal’s birdwatchers help monitor wildlife and promote tourism
entry.content:
KATHMANDU — As a child, Shankar Tiwari and his friends killed birds for fun around Chitwan National Park in central Nepal, where they grew up. Years later, a foreign guest at the hotel where Tiwari worked took him birdwatching and turned the hunter into a bird lover.

The striking yellow and black plumage and red eyes of the black-hooded oriole (Oriolus xanthornus), which he saw magnified through binoculars for the first time, sparked Tiwari’s lifelong passion for birds, he said. Today, the 57-year-old is one of Nepal’s leading birdwatching guides and a prominent member of the country’s growing birdwatching community that is contributing to bird conservation while promoting it as a tourism attraction.

“The birdwatching community has grown significantly today,” he said. “This has helped not just in raising awareness of the birds, but the community also helps in keeping tabs on the birds — how their habitat and population have changed over the years.”

A newstudysuggests that birdwatching is becoming increasingly popular in Nepal, particularly among the young, and that this trend “contributes to biodiversity conservation through public engagement and ecological data collection.” In Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, nonprofits like Bird Conservation Nepal (BCN) and Friends of Birds organize events on weekends, drawing a diverse group of birdwatchers.

entry.content:
Bird Flu Spreading Rapidly in Kathmandu, Affecting Poultry and Raising Health Concerns

Bird flu (avian influenza) is spreading rapidly across Kathmandu Valley, affecting poultry farms and wild bird populations. Health authorities have confirmed multiple outbreaks in commercial poultry operations across Bhaktapur, Lalitpur, and Kathmandu districts. The Department of Livestock Services has ordered culling of thousands of birds in affected zones and established quarantine perimeters. Public health officials are monitoring poultry workers for symptoms while emphasizing that transmission to humans remains rare. The outbreak comes during peak summer when wild migratory patterns and high-density urban poultry farming create conditions for rapid viral spread.

entry.title: Nepal’s new government bets on tax revenue over clean energy push
entry.summary: Nepal’s new government bets on tax revenue over clean energy push
entry.content:
KATHMANDU — When Balendra Shah took office as Nepal’s new prime minister in March following a landslide victory for his party, he inherited a fuel crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. His government faced a choice between speeding up the clean energy transition or shoring up the public finances needed to sustain it. In its May 29 fiscal policy, it chose the latter.

Nepal imports fossil fuels at a cost of 300 billion rupees ($2 billion) a year, including cooking gas that it subsidizes about 9 billion rupees ($59.5 million) annually. On the “clean” side of that equation, nearly all its grid electricity comes from hydropower — so much so that it exports the surplus to India and Bangladesh during the wet season. And on sales of electric vehicles,Nepal ranks second globally, with EVs estimated to account for 73% of new car sales in 2025, thanks to lower import taxes compared to internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles.

But the new government argues for a shift to raise revenue to fund grid upgrades that would make a clean energy transition possible in the first place. A former bureaucrat and a sitting official both told Mongabay that this logic is backward: that the tax revenue raised will be less than the savings in gas subsidies if it instead encouraged households to switch to electric stoves.

In his maiden budget speech, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle announced a 5% value-added tax on high-consuming electricity users, and fresh new taxes on EV imports. The prime minister said the government needs the money: “We need funds for strengthening the [electricity] transmission system and VAT is for that purpose,” Shah told parliament on June 1.

This marks a shift in the policy direction of the past two decades, endorsed by successive governments, and even by Shah’s Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) in its own March election manifesto. entry.title: Tiger Island: Inside Nepal's Record-Breaking Tiger Sanctuary
entry.summary: On a small island in western Nepal's Bardiya National Park, one of the highest concentrations of tigers on Earth is rewriting what we know about these elusive predators — captured on film for the first time by an armada of drones.
entry.content:
Tiger Island: Inside Nepal's Record-Breaking Tiger Sanctuary

On a small, tangled island in the river systems of western Nepal, something extraordinary is happening. Bardiya National Park is now home to one of the highest concentrations of tigers anywhere on Earth — and for the first time, a BBC film crew has captured their hidden lives using an unprecedented fleet of drones.

Goma, the matriarch tigress of Tiger Island. BBC/Tiger Island

The Discovery

In 2023, wildlife filmmaker Patrick Evans was in Nepal filming rhinos for the BBC series Asia when he received a tip from his executive producer: Bardiya National Park had seen a sixfold increase in tiger numbers. The BBC News Nepal team had been there and documented a remarkable recovery. But filming tigers is notoriously difficult — one crew spent over 700 days following tigers without once capturing them hunting.

Evans flew across Nepal to see for himself. Within two days, he saw three tigers. "I count this as my first real sighting," he wrote, "because I was able to see its blazing eyes. I found myself truly shocked at its enormous size — it felt comparable to watching a horse crossing the landscape."

That encounter launched a two-year project that became Tiger Island, a groundbreaking BBC documentary that used an entire fleet of drones to follow individual tigers through two separate months of filming — a world first for wildlife filmmaking.

Drone footage and remote cameras revealed unprecedented tiger behaviour. BBC/Tiger Island

Meet the Tigers

The crew identified individual tigers by their stripe patterns — nature's barcodes, unique to each animal. Here are the residents of Tiger Island:

Goma — The nine-year-old matriarch. Estimated to be the largest and most experienced tigress on the island, Goma has successfully raised multiple litters to adulthood. Local wildlife guides Sushila and Manju Mahatara named her after their grandmother and have observed her for years. At the time of filming, she had two nine-month-old cubs.

Mala — Goma's four-year-old daughter. Typically, young tigers leave their mothers at around two years of age. Mala inherited part of her mother's territory — a common behaviour among solitary big cats where mothers cede territory to daughters to minimise conflict. As a first-time mother with three cubs aged just three months, Mala faced a steep learning curve.

Jugini — Possibly another daughter of Goma's, and her neighbour to the north. She interacts peacefully with the other tigresses, especially Goma. At the time of filming, Jugini had three cubs of her own.

Bandheil — The only known male tiger controlling territory on the island. Adult male tigers in Nepal typically exceed 200 kilograms, and Bandheil is one of the largest seen in the area. Male tigers defend territories up to 18 miles across and may not play a role in cub-rearing — and may even kill cubs they encounter.

Bandheil, the dominant male, controls territory across the entire island. BBC/Tiger Island

Technology Meets Conservation

What makes Tiger Island unique is the technology behind it. The crew deployed an entire fleet of drones — a world-first approach for tiger filming — allowing them to follow individual animals through dense vegetation that would be impossible to navigate on foot. Remote camera traps supplemented the aerial footage, building a detailed picture of the tigers' movements, relationships, and hunting strategies.

The drone footage revealed behaviours never documented before: tender moments between Goma and her cubs, tense encounters between rival tigresses, and the extraordinary distances Bandheil covers in a single night — up to 18 miles.

Nepal's Conservation Success

Bardiya's tiger recovery is one of the world's great conservation stories. Nepal nearly doubled its tiger population between 2010 and 2022, from 121 to 355 individuals, putting it on track to meet the global TX2 goal of doubling wild tiger numbers. Bardiya alone saw its tiger population increase sixfold.

The success is built on community-based conservation. Local guides like the Mahatara sisters — Sushila, Manju, and Ranju — are central to both the research and the filming. Their intimate knowledge of individual tigers, passed down through years of patient observation, made the BBC's work possible.

The sisters carry stout wooden sticks as their only defense while walking barefoot through tiger territory — a powerful reminder that Nepal's conservation success depends on people living alongside predators at close quarters.

What's Next

With Goma confirmed to have mated with Bandheil, a new generation of cubs will soon arrive on Tiger Island. The BBC team plans to return, documenting how the next chapter unfolds for Nepal's most famous tiger family.

Tiger Island and the Asia episode "Tangled Worlds" are available on BBC iPlayer. For Nepal, it's a story of what's possible when conservation, technology, and local knowledge come together — and proof that even the most elusive animals can reveal their secrets when we find new ways of looking.

Sources: BBC — Meet the Tigers | BBC — Tiger Island: An Origin Story

entry.title: What’s jimbu? The herb that bolsters an iconic Nepali dish could also help save snow leopards
entry.summary: What’s jimbu? The herb that bolsters an iconic Nepali dish could also help save snow leopards
entry.content:
KATHMANDU — In Nepal, there’s a popular saying: “dal bhat power, 24 hour.” It refers to a humble plateful of rice and soupy lentils that Nepalis swear by, both at home and across the diaspora. It’s fuel for the body and a taste of home where it’s a staple meal for lunch and dinner. Now, an aromatic herb from the Himalayas that gives the Nepali staple its distinctive flavor offers Indigenous communities a potential promise: An alternative source of income and fewer conflicts with the iconic snow leopards that live in these mountain peaks.

How so? The residents of Phu Valley who cultivate jimbu (Allium przewalskianum) in this high-altitude settlement, located in the trans-Himalayan region of Manang that borders China’s Tibet region will tell you. They grow this herb, also known as Himalayan chive, as a cash crop — and as a way to help save “the big cat of the mountains.” Dried jimbu is usually fried in ghee, or clarified butter, and poured over simmering dal for an earthy flavor.

“Whenever we talk about dal bhat, the most famous of them all is the Thakali version prepared by the Thakali communities of the mountains,” said Shailendra Thakali, an expert in environmental conservation, tourism and livelihoods, referring to a version of the dish made by Indigenous people known for their traditional cuisines. “And the Thakali dal bhat owes its unique taste and aroma to jimbu,” Thakali added.

Until recently, residents foraged this herb from steep, risky slopes. They used some in their own cooking and sold whatever was left, because it fetches large sums, with growing demand in Nepal and beyond. In 2022, the Narpa Bhumi Rural Municipality — where Phu village is located — partnered withMountain Spirit, a Nepal-based NGO, to launch a pilot project to domesticate jimbu in nearby abandoned farmland, turning it into a community asset.

entry.title: How snow leopards, wolves and leopards share the same Himalayan valley, study
entry.summary: How snow leopards, wolves and leopards share the same Himalayan valley, study
entry.content:
Three of Asia’s most formidable predators share territory in a remote Nepal valley by eating different prey, according to a new study. Researchers found that diet, not time or space, is what keeps snow leopards (Panthera uncia), common leopards (Panthera pardus), and Himalayan wolves (Canis lupus chanco) from coming into direct conflict.

Thestudy, published inPLOS One, drew on more than six years of camera-trapping and scat analysis in the Lapchi Valley of the Gaurishankar Conservation Area in Nepal’ s central Himalayas. Researchers set 26 cameras across the landscape over three survey periods between 2018 and 2025 and identified each predator’s diet by analyzing fecal DNA and examining prey hair under a microscope.

Snow leopards, they found, fed mainly on wild ungulates, including blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur), musk deer (Moschus leucogaster), Himalayan tahr (Hemitragus jemlahicus), and Himalayan serow (Capricornis sumatraensis). Blue sheep alone made up nearly half their diet.

Himalayan wolves ate a mix of wild prey like blue sheep and musk deer as well as livestock such as goats, horses, and yaks (Bos grunniens).

Leopards relied heavily on livestock and animals associated with human settlements, including dogs, though barking deer (Muntiacus muntjak) and goral (Naemorhedus goral) also appeared in their scats.

Snow leopards and wolves shared roughly three-quarters of their prey, far more than either shared with leopards. Of the three, snow leopards had the narrowest diet, concentrating on wild ungulates. Leopards ranged most widely, and wolves fell in between, switching between wild prey and livestock depending on what was available. All three predators were active mostly at night and used overlapping terrain.
